To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) The stray force noise of the capacitive sensor surrounding a LISA Pathfinder-type test mass can be measured to a level below 1 mHz/Hz, 2) The excess force noise is below the thermal noise of a fused silica torsion pendulum over a wide frequency range, 3) The stray force measurement is dominated by the noise of the capacitors, and 4) A new torsion pendulums based on higher quality factor fused silica fibers is developed,

the excess noise of the capacitive position sensors in LISA and LISP is at the level of the thermal noise of the pendulum suspension at frequencies below 0.1 Hz, and that the excess noise is at the level or below the thermal noise of a high quality factor fused silica torsion pendulum suspension at higher frequencies.

the stray forces in capacitive position sensors can be reduced to the LISA Pathfinder requirement, and that this requirement is not a fundamental limit, as higher quality factor torsion pendulums can be used to reduce the stray forces further.
In summary, our research is concerned with
improving the sensitivity of the torsion pendulum measurement technique for testing the free-fall environment of LISA test masses.

the development and testing of a torsion pendulum that will allow for the first time to measure the stray forces arising from capacitive position sensors with the precision required to verify the free-fall of LISA test masses on ground and in space.
the design and development of a new torsion pendula, based on fused silica fibers, which will enable a more stringent test of free-fall.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, with the current technology, it is possible to achieve a level of force sensitivity with a torsion pendulum that is compatible with LISA Pathfinder.

a fused silica pendulum with a torsion fiber with a Q-factor of at least 1×107, with a length of at least 2 m, can be used to verify the LISA Pathfinder goal for the force noise in the test mass-sensor interaction.

the fused silica pendulums have demonstrated that the capacitive sensor can be used to detect forces on the test mass with sufficient precision to allow the LISA Pathfinder mission to achieve its goal.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we can now test the limits of free fall with a precision of 10-14 N at 1 mHz and 10-13 N at 1 Hz, which is sufficient to test the LISA requirements.
the fused silica torsion fiber is a promising candidate material for the suspension fiber in LISA.
the LISA Pathfinder goal of a 10−14 N/Hz1/2 force sensitivity can be achieved in the range of 1 mHz to 1 Hz, with the possibility of further improvements in the 1 Hz to 10 Hz frequency range.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a torsion pendulum can be a powerful tool in the quest for the ultimate limits of free-falls, and that it can be used to test the limits of free falls with a sensitivity approaching the LISA Pathfinder requirements.

the fused silica pendulums are a promising tool for testing the limits for the stray forces arising from the interaction between the test masses and the capacitive sensor, and thus for testing the performance of the capacitive position sensors.
the torsion pendulum is a viable technique for measuring excess force noise at the required levels for LISA Pathfinder and, with some further improvements, for LISA.
